description: We are a multidisciplinary 6-member team from the UAE tackling the ultimate space challenge: identifying and analyzing extreme Earth locations that serve as geological and environmental analogs for permanent Moon and Mars base sites. Combining data science, systems development, and space tech passion, our squad is fully set. Let's engineer the future of interplanetary habitation together!
summary:
Borrowed Terrain is an interactive atlas that explores how two sites in Sharjah, UAE, could help rover teams rehearse for the Moon and Mars. We used open elevation data from NASA’s Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, alongside Landsat imagery and published Perseverance observations.

For the Moon, users can change the light angle and direction to compare modeled shadows at the Fāyah ridge and dune apron, the eastern Hajar fan, and Malapert Massif. At a simulated light elevation of 5°, the ridge and apron showed more modeled shadow than the fan in all eight directions. That makes the ridge and apron a promising candidate for testing how rover cameras handle transitions between light and shadow.

For Mars, a 3.96 km elevation profile across the eastern Hajar fan shows a gradual downhill trend. Our comparison with Jezero Crater shows why rover teams need close-up views of sediment layers to test whether deposits formed in a lake.

By showing what each site can help test and where the comparison breaks down, Borrowed Terrain helps mission teams choose Earth rehearsal sites for specific rover tasks.
details:
Borrowed Terrain is a browser-based atlas that compares two sites in Sharjah, UAE, with terrain on the Moon and Mars. We developed it remotely using public elevation data, satellite imagery, and published rover observations. The atlas runs in a web browser using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used Python and GDAL to process the elevation data and calculate the terrain results.

For the lunar comparison, we resampled NASA SRTM and lunar LOLA elevation data to approximately 30 m. Our model scans the local terrain horizon in eight directions and marks a cell as shadowed when surrounding terrain blocks the selected light angle. Users can change the angle and direction and see the maps update. At 5°, the Fāyah ridge and dune apron had more modeled shadow than the eastern Hajar fan in all eight directions. That makes the ridge and apron a candidate for rehearsing how rover cameras handle transitions between sunlight and shadow. We considered elevation error, grid resolution, and the difference between a controlled lighting scenario and real sunlight in Sharjah.

For the Mars comparison, we extracted 133 elevation samples along a 3.96 km transect of the eastern Hajar alluvial fan. The profile falls from 186 m to 164 m. We compared this gradual decline with published Perseverance observations of sedimentary layers at Kodiak in Jezero Crater. The atlas shows how an elevation profile can guide where to look and how closer rover observations help test whether sediments were deposited in a lake.

The same region can support two different rehearsals. Borrowed Terrain helps teams choose an Earth site based on the rover task and understand which parts of the comparison can transfer to the Moon or Mars.
